date_label: June–October 1893, Oxford and Goring (Grainger in Wilde's service)
summary: Walter Grainger, about sixteen by Wilde's sworn estimate, was a servant at the house in High Street, Oxford, where Douglas had rooms; in June-July 1893 Wilde brought him to 'The Cottage' at Goring as under-butler, where he remained until Wilde left in October. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at both places; the allegation was never charged and Grainger never gave evidence. Carson's pressing of Wilde's flippant answer — that he never kissed Grainger because he was 'a peculiarly plain boy' — is recorded by Hyde as the climax of the cross-examination.

disputed.claim: that Wilde solicited Walter Grainger to commit sodomy and committed acts of gross indecency with him at Oxford (June 1893) and at 'The Cottage,' Goring (June-Aug 1893)
disputed.disputed_by: Wilde's sworn denials ('No indecencies ever took place between myself and Grainger'; 'I never on any occas[i]on asked him to come into my bedroom')
disputed.grounds: allegation stands in the plea alone: never charged (outside CCC jurisdiction — Hyde p. 256) and no testimony from Grainger is printed in Hyde; the record's age statement (sixteen) is Wilde's own sworn answer at the libel trial

sources.quote: Do you know Walter Grainger?—Yes. How old is he?—He was about sixteen when I knew him. He was a servant at a certain house in High Street, Oxford, where Lord Alfred Douglas had rooms. I have stayed there several times. Grainger waited at table. … Did you ever kiss him?—Oh, dear no. He was a peculiarly plain boy. He was, unfortunately, extremely ugly. I pitied him for it.

sources.quote: CARSON: Did you know Walter Grainger? WILDE: Yes. CARSON: What was he? WILDE: A servant at Lord Alfred Douglas's rooms in Oxford. … CARSON: How old was he? WILDE: I should think about sixteen. … CARSON: Were you on familiar terms with Grainger? WILDE: What do you mean by 'familiar terms'? CARSON: I mean to say did you have him to dine with you or anything of that kind? WILDE: Never in my life. CARSON: What? WILDE: No! It is really trying to ask me such a question. No, of course not. He waited on me at table; he did not dine with me. … CARSON: Did you ever kiss him? WILDE: Oh, no, never in my life; he was a peculiarly plain boy. CARSON: He was what? sources.context: Carson's cross-examination, Thursday morning 4 April 1895. Compare Hyde 1948 p. 150, which renders the same exchange as continuous narrative answers and gives 'Oh, dear no.' where the shorthand has 'Oh, no, never in my life'. Hyde also omits the 'familiar terms' exchange entirely, and smooths Wilde's broken self-correction under Carson's interruption into the finished sentence 'He was, unfortunately, extremely ugly. I pitied him for it.' The quote ends mid-sentence because the page does.
